Attachment Security and Trust within Dyadic, Group, Sociopolitical, and
Spiritual/Religious Relationships
Mario Mikulincer
Baruch Ivcher School of Psychology
Reichman University
Phillip R. Shaver
Department of Psychology
University of California, Davis
2
Abstract
Attachment theory has become one of the most influential theories in psychology,
generating an explosion of empirical research and clinical applications. At the heart of the theory
is a conception of security dynamics, a set of psychological processes involved in the search for
social sources of safety and security in the context of threats and challenges, and the implications
of felt security for emotional stability and personal growth. In this chapter, we focus on the role
that security dynamics play in shaping a person's sense of trust while showing that trust is an
integral part of felt security. We review evidence that feeling secure with respect to the support
of close relationship partners, experts or leaders in particular domains (e.g., teachers, managers,
therapists), social groups or organizations (e.g., teamwork, workplace), or supernatural figures
(e.g., God) contributes to the development of trust in the benevolence, reliability, dependability,
and credibility of these and other figures.
Keywords: Attachment, trust, responsiveness, interpersonal relationships, social relationships,
group processes, spirituality
3
Overview
Attachment theory (Bowlby, 1982) is one of the leading frameworks for understanding
emotion regulation, mental health, and the quality of personal and social relationships. At the
heart of the theory is a conception of security dynamics, a set of psychological processes
involved in the search for social sources of security in the context of threats and challenges, and
the consequences of security attainment for emotional stability and personal growth. Simply
stated, actual or anticipated dangers, threats, and challenges motivate a person to seek the
proximity and support of competent and benevolent others and rely on them to help restore
emotional balance and confidently pursue personal goals. Being well cared for by these figures, a
person develops a sense of attachment security or what Sroufe and Waters (1977) called felt
security – confidence that one is worthy and lovable and that others will be supportive when
needed. This inner sense facilitates effective emotion regulation, contributes to mental health and
personal and social adjustment, sustains harmonious relationships, and favors the endorsement of
constructive means of conflict resolution at both interpersonal, intragroup, and intergroup levels
(Mikulincer & Shaver, 2016, 2023). Failure to attain felt security leaves distress unresolved and
interferes with emotion regulation and the quality of personal and social relationships.
In this chapter, we focus on the role that security dynamics play in shaping one's sense of
trust – the generalized expectancy that others can be relied on (Rotter, 1980), which is central to
healthy personal and social relationships (Simpson, 2007). We show that trust in other people
originates in early attachment relationships and that interpersonal trust is an integral part of felt
security. Specifically, we review evidence that people who feel secure with respect to close
relationship partners (e.g., parents, friends, romantic partners), experts or leaders in particular
domains (e.g., teachers, managers, therapists), informal or formal social groups, sociopolitical
4
entities (e.g., large organizations, social institutions), or supernatural figures (e.g., God) are
likely to trust in the reliability, dependability, and credibility of these and other figures. The
chapter includes also future directions in the study of the contribution of security dynamics to the
sense of trust.
Security Dynamics: The Search for Social Sources of Protection and Support
According to attachment theory (Bowlby, 1982), human beings are born with an evolved
psychobiological system ( attachment behavioral system) that motivates them to seek proximity
to supportive others ( attachment figures) in times of need and rely on them for dealing with
dangers, threats, and challenges. In Bowlby's (1982) view, attachment figures are special
individuals or social entities (e.g., groups) that are perceived to be benevolent and competent and
therefore to be potential sources of protection, support, and encouragement when needed. People
turn to attachment figures for two main provisions: A physical and emotional safe haven (i.e.,
which alleviates fears and distress) and a secure base from which to explore, learn, and thrive in
a confident manner (Ainsworth, 1991). The goal of proximity seeking is twofold – to feel
protected and comforted by an attachment figure when threatened and to feel that one's strivings
for competence and autonomy are validated, supported, and empowered by this figure.
Bowlby (1982, 1988) believed that the search for a safe haven and secure base, which is
critical for survival during infancy, continues to operate throughout life, as indicated by adults'
needs for affection, support, and encouragement when facing threats or challenges (Zeifman &
Hazan, 2016) and by their intense grief reactions following the loss of an attachment figure at
any age. However, bids for proximity and support may operate somewhat differently at different
ages despite the need for a safe haven and a secure base being important across the lifespan. For
example, the identity of targeted attachment figures tends to change with development. During
5
infancy, primary caregivers (usually parents or parent substitutes) typically occupy the role of
attachment figures (Ainsworth, 1991). However, during adolescence and adulthood, research
indicates that additional relationship partners also become potential attachment figures, including
close friends and romantic partners (Zeifman & Hazan, 2016).
Beyond these relationship partners, a wide variety of people can be perceived as
benevolent and competent figures to whom one can target bids for proximity and support in
particular contexts. These figures include teachers, coaches, and mentors in educational and
recreational settings, managers in work settings, officers in the military, therapists in clinical
settings, healthcare workers in medical settings, clergy in religion-related settings, and leaders in
social and political organizations. Research indicates that children, adolescents, and adults tend
to rely on one or more of these people, depending on circumstances, for obtaining a safe haven
and secure base (e.g., Mallinckrodt et al., 2009; Mayseless & Pooper, 2019; Sabol & Pianta,
2012). There is also evidence that other individuals and social entities can be recruited as
potential attachment figures, including pets, groups, social organizations and institutions, and
God (e.g., Granqvist, 2020; Mayseless & Popper, 2007; Smith et al., 1999; Zilcha-Mano et al.,
2011).
Attachment-Figure Responsiveness, Felt Security, and Insecure Forms of Attachment
Although all human beings are born with the capacity to seek proximity to and rely on
attachment figures in times of need, important individual differences arise in the context of
relationships with these figures from birth on. According to Bowlby (1973), these individual
differences are shaped by reactions of attachment figures to one's bids for proximity and support
in times of need and from storing memories of these reactions in the form of mental
representations of self and others ( internal working models). Interactions with attachment figures
6
who are sensitive and responsive to one's bids for proximity and support and who are capable of
providing the needed safe haven and secure base promote a sense of attachment security and
contribute to positive working models of self as worthy and competent and of others as kind and
caring (Bowlby, 1973). When a person's attachment figures are not reliably available and
supportive, however, the person's sense of lovability, competence, and worth is shaky or absent;
others' kindness and reliable caring are in doubt; and the person becomes less secure in personal
and social relationships and less confident in dealing with threats and challenges.
Pursuing these theoretical ideas in studies of adults, many researchers have focused on a
person's attachment orientation or attachment style, a systematic pattern of relational
expectations, emotions, and behaviors that results from a particular history of interactions with
attachment figures (Fraley & Shaver, 2000). These orientations can be conceptualized as regions
in a continuous two-dimensional space (e.g., Brennan et al., 1998). One dimension, attachment-
related avoidance, reflects the extent to which a person disbelieves others' benevolence and
defensively strives to maintain independence and emotional distance within personal and social
relationships. The other dimension, attachment anxiety, reflects the extent to which a person
worries that others will not be available or responsive in times of need and therefore engages in
overly demanding, intrusive, and even coercive bids for proximity and support. A person's
general attachment orientation can be viewed as the top node in a complex network of
attachment representations, some of which apply only to specific people and relationships and
others of which apply only in certain relational contexts (Mikulincer & Shaver, 2016). These
more specific mental representations can be activated by actual or imagined encounters with
supportive or unsupportive others even if they are incongruent with the dominant attachment
orientation (Mikulincer & Shaver, 2016).
7
Mikulincer and Shaver (2016) have proposed that individuals' location in the two-
dimensional anxiety-by-avoidance space reflects both their sense of attachment security and the
ways in which they deal with threats and challenges. People who score low on both insecurity
dimensions are generally secure, hold positive working models of self and others, and tend to
employ constructive and effective affect-regulation strategies. Those who score high on either
attachment anxiety or avoidance, or both, suffer from attachment insecurities and worries and
tend to use secondary attachment strategies that we, following Cassidy and Kobak (1988),
characterize as attachment-system “hyperactivation” or “deactivation” in the context of threats,
frustrations, rejections, and losses. People who score high on attachment anxiety rely on
hyperactivating strategies – energetic attempts to achieve support and love combined with lack
of confidence that these desired resources will be provided and with feelings of anger and
despair when they are not provided (Cassidy & Kobak, 1988). In contrast, people who score high
on attachment-related avoidance tend to use deactivating strategies, attempting not to seek
proximity to others when threatened, denying vulnerability and a need for other people, and
avoiding closeness and interdependence in relationships.
Bowlby (1988) summarized the adaptive benefits of a well-functioning, effective
attachment system. First, interactions with a security-enhancing attachment figure help a person
to down-regulate negative emotions and maintain stability in times of need or stress (Bowlby,
1973). Second, such interactions facilitate the cultivation of personal skills and talents, because a
child or adult who feels adequately protected and supported has greater courage and more
conflict-free attentional resources to engage in free play, curiously investigate objects and
environments, and develop affiliative relationships with peers. In the next section, we focus on
the implications of felt security for relational trust.
8
Attachment Security and Relational Trust
Trust is one of the most important qualities in personal and social relationships and is a
necessary condition for developing pro-relational feelings and beliefs that contribute to
commitment to and investment in a relationship and to its sustenance over time (Simpson, 2007).
Drawing on interdependence theory, Rempel et al. (1985) defined relational trust as involving (a)
the appraisal of others as reliable and predictable, (b) the belief that others are concerned with
one's needs and can be counted on in times of need, and (c) feelings of confidence in the strength
of the relationship (see also Chapter xx). These appraisals, beliefs and feelings seem to be
fortified whenever a relationship partner's responses meet one's needs and to be weakened when
these responses are not sensitive or responsive to one's needs. In the latter case, the partner's
responses tend to be perceived as a betrayal or breach of trust (Holmes & Rempel, 1989). This
conceptualization of relational trust implies that trust is an integral part of the construct of
security dynamics, and, like the sense of attachment security, it depends on the responsiveness
and supportiveness of others and their willingness and capacity to provide a safe haven and
secure base when needed.
Relational trust includes positive expectations about others' dependability in times of
need as well as about their kindness and caring. These expectations are the core components of
an attachment-secure person's working models of others (Mikulincer & Shaver, 2016). During
interactions with an attachment figure who effectively meets their needs for protection, comfort,
support, and encouragement, an attachment-secure person learns about the kindness of this figure
and forms positive expectations about his or her dependability when needed. Numerous studies
have shown that individuals who score lower on attachment anxiety and avoidance (i.e., those
who possess a sense of attachment security) have more positive explicit and implicit views of
9
others, hold more positive expectations concerning a relationship partner's behavior, and tend to
explain a partner's negative behavior in more positive, forgiving terms (see Mikulincer &
Shaver, 2016, for a review).
Furthermore, during these security-enhancing interactions, people acquire a relational
prototype or a “secure-base script” (Waters & Waters, 2006). This script contains something like
the following if-then propositions: “If I encounter an obstacle, threat, or challenge and/or become
distressed, I can approach an attachment figure for safe-haven or secure-base support; he or she
is likely to be emotionally available, sensitive, responsive, and capable of providing a safe haven
and a secure base; I will feel calm, comforted, and empowered as a result of approaching this
figure; I can then confidently return to other activities.” The construction of this script within a
particular relationship or across different relational contexts increases confidence that others will
be available and supportive in times of need. As a result, a sense of relational trust is formed, and
the attachment-secure person can remain emotionally stable when confronting threats and
challenges because he or she can count on others' responsiveness and support if autonomous
coping efforts fail.
Felt security and relational trust are very closely related, if not synonymous. Attachment
security comes from trusting that attachment figures will be available or responsive when needed
or desired. And trusting a particular relationship partner (or group or God) is formed during
comforting and empowering interactions with this figure that promote and sustain positive
models of the self and others and infuse felt security.
The attachment basis of relational trust can be observed during interactions of children
with their caregivers. According to Bosmans (2016), children learn to trust in a caregiver when
he or she gets associated with the experience of comfort and relief following a caregiver's
10
successful provision of support in the context of distress. In a direct test of this proposition,
Vandevivere et al. (2018) conducted an experiment in which school-age children, ranging in age
from 9 to 13 years old, watched a distress-inducing video and their mothers were instructed
either to (a) remain in another room, (b) stay in the same room with their child but refrain from
offering emotional support, or (c) provide emotional support to their child during the video.
Findings indicated that children whose mothers were responsive to their needs reported greater
trust in their mother (e.g., “At this moment, I feel that I can count on my mother to help me if I
encounter a problem”) than children whose mother was absent or only physically but not
psychologically available during the video. Further supportive evidence has been provided by
Bosmans et al. (2019), who exposed elementary-school children to an unfamiliar adult who
could assist them in solving a challenging task. Bosman et al. (2019) manipulated the degree to
which the support offered by this adult was helpful. As expected, children who were presented
with an unfamiliar adult who provided more effective support developed more trust in that
person.
Overall, these findings indicate that security-enhancing interactions promote relational
trust and imply that people who possess a solid sense of attachment security are likely to
habitually trust others and perceive them as benevolent, reliable, and dependable figures. Indeed,
there is evidence that more attachment-secure adolescents and adults are more likely to judge
unfamiliar, computer-generated faces as trustworthy and to behave in a trusting, cooperative
manner in social dilemma games (e.g., Martinez et al., 2021; McClure et al., 2013). Interestingly,
this heightened trust seems to be generalized even to non-human figures. Recently, Gillath et al.
(2021) found that lower scores on an attachment anxiety measure (i.e., greater security) predicted
greater trust in artificial intelligence. And experimental activation of a sense of attachment
11
security (versus activation of positive affect or neutral feelings) increased trust in artificial
intelligence. In the following sections, we review evidence showing that this link between
attachment security and trust can also observed in the context not only of dyadic relationships
but also one's relationships with social groups and organizations and spiritual figures.
4.1 Romantic Relationships
Theoretically, a person's attachment security with respect to a romantic partner or spouse
bolsters optimistic expectations that this partner will be responsive to one's bids for protection
and support when needed and unlikely to betray one's trust. With these positive views of a
romantic partner, it is relatively easy for a secure person to move from a cautious, not quite
trusting, somewhat self-protective stance early in a relationship to a more confident, trusting,
emotionally engaged, and pro-relational stance. When a person feels secure with respect to a
romantic partner, based on previous supportive interactions with this partner, he or she can
openly express needs to the partner, fully commit to and invest in the relationship, and make any
compromise or sacrifice needed to sustain relationship satisfaction and longevity.
This relational process is the focus of Reis and Shaver's (1988) model of the formation of
high-quality relationships. The process begins when one partner (A) reveals personally
significant aspects of him- or herself to the other partner (B). Subsequent steps in the process are
shaped by partner B's responsiveness. B's understanding, validating, and caring response
facilitates A's expression of deeper personal needs and concerns and enhances his or her sense of
trust in the partner's goodwill and investment in the relationship. These positive relational
feelings and attitudes lead partner A to be sensitive and responsive to partner B's expression of
needs and feelings, which, in turn, augment partner B's trust and pro-relational attitudes. In this
way, a mutual, self-amplifying cycle of responsiveness, trust, and commitment is formed, which
12
strengthens the felt security of both partners and the quality of their relationship. In contrast, a
distant, disapproving, or rejecting response interferes with the formation of relational trust and
impairs this relationship-promotion cycle. There is a large body of evidence showing that a
partner's responsiveness contributes greatly to trust within romantic relationships (e.g.,
Canevello &Crocker, 2010; Shallcross & Simpson, 2012; Wieselquist et al., 1999).
In adult attachment research, the link between attachment security and relational trust
within romantic relationships was evident from the beginning in Hazan and Shaver's (1987)
pioneering study of romantic love viewed as an attachment process. As Campbell and Stanton
(2019) noted, “the first measure of adult attachment created by Hazan and Shaver contained both
indirect and direct references to trust (e.g., 'I often worry that my partner doesn't really love me
or won't want to stay with me.' [anxious], 'I find it difficult to trust them [partners]
completely…' [avoidant]), highlighting the theoretical importance of trust to conceptualizing
individual differences in attachment” (p. 149) (see all Chapter xx). Moreover, people who
classified themselves as secure with respect to attachment were more likely than those who were
insecure (anxious or avoidant) to report that their romantic relationships were friendly, warm,
trusting, and supportive. Whereas avoidant individuals' negative working models of others run
counter to relational trust, attachment-anxious individuals are plagued by doubts about their
partner's trustworthiness and remain vigilant for signs of a partner's unavailability, making it
difficult for them to approach their partners in a confident, trusting manner.
These initial findings were replicated in subsequent studies that relied on continuous
measures of attachment orientations: Adults who score lower on attachment anxiety or avoidance
scales (i.e., who are more secure with respect to attachment) tend to report more trust within their
romantic relationships and describe their partner as more trustworthy (e.g., Rodriguez et al.,
13
2021). Also, individuals reporting lower levels of anxious or avoidant attachment have faster
access to comforting memories of a romantic partner's dependable behavior and report more
daily experiences in which their romantic partner behaved in a trustworthy manner over a 3-week
period (e.g., Mikulincer, 1998). In their 31-year longitudinal study, Klohnen and Bera (1998)
found that 52-year-old women with a self-reported secure attachment style had rated romantic
partners and spouses as more trustworthy at ages 27 and 43, and still did so at age 52, compared
with women who were insecure with respect to attachment. Interestingly, Feeney (2002) found
that insecure people's appraisal of a spouse's untrustworthiness tended to increase with length of
marriage, probably because “…insecure spouses become less optimistic about their relationships
across the marital life cycle and more attuned to potential signs of negativity and rejection” (p.
51).
Further evidence concerning the link between attachment security and trust is provided
by studies of reactions to a romantic partner's betrayal of trust (Mikulincer, 1998; Jang et al.,
2002). More secure people are more likely to talk openly with their partner about his or her
deception and find ways to restore relationship harmony. In contrast, attachment-anxious people
are more likely to ruminate about their partner's betrayal, avoid discussing the partner's
deception, and react with strong negative emotions. Avoidant individuals increase their distance
from the transgressing partner and tend to deny the importance of the threatening episode.
However, Mikulincer (1998) measured lexical decision times to the word “worry” and found that
avoidant people implicitly activated the word “worry” when primed with a trust-violation story.
This discrepancy between self-reports of not being bothered by betrayal and implicit signs of
worry seems to be a manifestation of the fragile nature of avoidant people's defenses (Mikulincer
& Shaver, 2016).
14
Mikulincer (1998) provided evidence concerning the goals related to establishing a sense
of relational trust. As compared to attachment-secure participants, attachment-anxious ones were
more likely to report trusting a romantic partner as a means of gaining his or her love and
support, and they displayed readier access to security-related thoughts after being primed with
sentences reflecting a partner's trustworthiness (faster lexical decision times for security-related
words). These findings reflect attachment-anxious individuals' unmet needs for closeness and
security. In contrast, avoidant people viewed expressions of relational trust as manipulative
means to control their romantic partner's behavior (“If I trust you, you should trust me and allow
me to do what I want”). These reactions seem to be an indication of avoidant people's desire for
social dominance and control.
Attachment-anxious people's lack of trust in their romantic partner is also manifested in
their tendency to engage in excessive reassurance seeking, the coercive demand that a partner
assure one that he or she will be available when needed (“If I can elicit assurances that my
partner loves me, I won't need to worry as much about rejection”). This tendency has been
documented in several correlational studies linking anxious attachment with reassurance seeking,
as reported by both the study participants themselves and their partners (e.g., Evraire et al.,
2014). In a 14-day diary study, Shaver et al. (2005) found that more attachment-anxious
participants sought more reassurance from their romantic partner following days on which they
experienced relationship conflicts than following days on which little or no conflict was reported.
It seems that attachment-anxious people seek reassurance as a way of quelling worries about
partner's untrustworthiness.
4.2 Other Dyadic Relationships
15
The attachment-trust link is also evident in friendships and sibling relationships (see
Chpater xx) during adolescence and adulthood. A host of studies have found that more
attachment-secure adolescents and young adults tend to report higher levels of trust, affection,
self-disclosure, mutuality, and satisfaction in their friendships and sibling relationships (e.g.,
Chow & Tan, 2013; Tibbetts & Scharfe, 2015). These findings have been replicated in the
analysis of virtual friendships on the Internet and actual interactions between friends in a
laboratory (e.g., Buote et al., 2009; Shomaker & Furman, 2009). For example, Shomaker and
Furman (2009) observed 200 adolescents discussing problems with their friend and found that
attachment security (as assessed by an interview) was associated with heightened self-disclosure
and mutuality while talking about their concerns and their friends' concerns.
There is also evidence that attachment-secure students form more trusting and close
relationships with their teachers than insecure students (see Sabol & Pianta, 2012, for a review).
For example, longitudinal data from the National Institute of Child Health and Human
Development Study of Early Child Care and Youth Development indicate that secure attachment
to mother in early childhood significantly predicts more harmonious and cooperative
relationships with a teacher at 54 months and in kindergarten, 1st grade, and 5th grade
(O'Connor & McCartney, 2006; O'Connor et al., 2012). In addition, children who are more
securely attached to mother tend to appraise teachers as more reliable, dependable, warm, and
supportive (see Ahnert et al., 2006, for a meta-analysis).
The link between attachment security and trust is also evident in the ways clients relate
to their therapist. First, clients of a more empathic and responsive therapist (as rated by clients or
external observers) not only feel more attachment-secure regarding the therapist but are also
more likely to form a trusting and cooperative relationship with him or her, which Bordin (1979)
16
called a solid therapist-client alliance (see Elliot et al., 2018, for a meta-analysis). In addition, as
compared to clients who score relatively high on attachment anxiety or avoidance prior to
therapy, more secure clients tend to trust their therapist's good intentions and to agree with him
or her regarding therapeutic tasks and goals (e.g., Coyne et al., 2018). However, meta-analytic
studies revealed that, although clients' pre-therapy attachment security makes a significant, albeit
mild, contribution to the strength of the therapist-client alliance, the felt security a client
gradually develops toward his or her therapist over therapy is the most important antecedent of
the alliance (e.g., Mallinckrodt & Jeong, 2015). Overall, these findings highlight the role clients'
attachment security plays in fostering a trusting therapist-client relationship and promoting
constructive therapeutic work.
In their attachment-informed model of health-related behavior, Hunter and Maunder
(2001) proposed that patients' attachment orientations are crucial for understanding the trust they
feel toward healthcare providers (e.g., physicians, nurses) and the quality of medical services
they receive. According to Hunter and Maunder (2001), avoidant patients' negative models of
others can cause them to distrust the intentions, knowledge, and skills of healthcare providers
and show disdain and contempt for them. This can then frustrate the medical team and cause
them to back away from avoidant patients. Patients scoring high on measures of attachment
anxiety might also have little confidence in the availability and responsiveness of healthcare
providers in times of need and therefore use various means to keep their medical team close by
and engaged (e.g., repeatedly complaining about physical problems, exaggerating their
helplessness and need). These anxious, controlling, and sometimes coercive proximity-seeking
behaviors may discourage and 'burn out' healthcare providers and make them reluctant to
approach the patient (Hunter & Maunder, 2001).
17
These ideas have been tested and supported in studies conducted in medical settings (e.g.,
McWilliams, 2018). For example, Holwerda et al. (2013) followed up cancer patients 3 and 9
months after their diagnosis and found that more attachment-insecure patients reported less trust
in their doctors. In another study, patients watched video-clips of consultations of oncologists
with cancer patients and findings indicated that more avoidant patients appraised the videotaped
oncologists as less trustworthy (Hillen et al., 2014).
In the context of follower-leader relationships, more attachment-insecure workers have
been found to appraise their manager as less trustworthy, supportive, and competent and to hold
more negative expectations concerning his or her responsiveness (e.g., Gruda & Kafetsios,
2020). Fein et al. (2020) conducted a meta-analysis of 10 studies of leader-follower exchanges in
the workplace and concluded that employees who are more attachment-secure in close
relationships are more likely to perceive their manager as a trustworthy person and to comply
with his or her instructions. Interestingly, pet owners who feel more attachment-secure with
respect to close relationship partners or to their pet tend to perceive their pet as more dependable
and to hold more positive expectations regarding the pet's responsiveness (e.g., Zilcha-Mano et
al., 2011).
4.3 Group Relationships
As in the case of dyadic relationships, perceptions of group members' benevolence and
competence (the two defining components of a security-enhancing attachment figure) are critical
for the formation of trust in a group and the adoption of a collaborative stance during group
interactions (Williams, 2001). According to Wildman et al. (2012), these perceptions are
influenced by what group members bring with them into a newly formed group, such as their
generalized propensity to hold positive expectations about others' intentions and behaviors and
18
to trust people even before meeting them. But it is actual interactions within the new group that
calibrate these perceptions and the level of trust toward the group. Specifically, members'
behaviors that are perceived to be kind, other-oriented, collaborative, and helpful within group
interactions contribute to the development of trust in the group. Over time, these pro-group
behaviors, coupled with one's perceptions of these behaviors, calibrates the degree to which one
believes the group to be dependable and the certainty that group members will behave in a
collaborative manner in the future (Wildman et al., 2012).
This theoretical analysis of trust formation within group relationships fits very well with
our attachment perspective on relational trust. As we noted in the previous section, the sense of
attachment security includes positive beliefs (working models) about others and inclines people
to extend trust to others in the absence of prior knowledge. As a result, attachment-secure people
may be more likely than attachment-insecure people to trust a newly formed group. In addition,
according to our attachment reasoning, this group-level trust can be further enhanced by positive
interactions with group members that are perceived to be responsive (understanding, validating,
caring) to each other's needs and to empower each other to learn and explore new alternatives
without fear of being rejected, excluded, or punished (secure-base support). These positive group
interactions then fortify members' within-group sense of attachment security (e.g., confidence
that group members' support will be available when needed; Rom & Mikulincer, 2003) and
enhance their level of trust in the group. Moreover, these positive interactions may counteract
attachment-insecure people's tendency to distrust others' goodwill and responsiveness, and this
may soften destructive relational tendencies aroused by attachment insecurities during group
interactions.
19
There is evidence that a person's sense of attachment security in close relationships can
positively bias group-level perceptions. Across four studies, Rom and Mikulincer (2003) found
that lower levels of attachment anxiety or avoidance in close relationships (greater security) were
associated with more positive views of social groups and more positive memories of group
interactions. Similar findings were reported by Smith et al. (1999) who assessed anxious
attachment to a group (e.g., “I often worry my group will not always want me as a member”) and
avoidant attachment to a group (e.g., “I prefer not to depend on my group”). Lower scores on
group attachment anxiety or avoidance predicted more positive evaluations of social groups (e.g.,
fraternities, sororities), and higher perceived support from groups. In addition, whereas group
attachment anxiety was associated with stronger negative emotions toward social groups, group
avoidant attachment was associated with lower levels of positive affect toward these groups.
Attachment insecurities in close relationships also seem to negatively bias relational
perceptions and attitudes during group therapy. For example, clients with higher levels of
attachment anxiety or avoidance (assessed before therapy) are more likely to provide negative
appraisals of group climate and togetherness during and after therapy (e.g., Lo Coco et al., 2016)
and to perceive lower levels of support from other group members during therapy (Harel et al.,
2011). In addition, more attachment-avoidant clients tend to devalue other group members'
disclosures during therapeutic sessions (Shechtman & Dvir, 2006).
In a recent theoretical article, Tropp (2021) applied attachment theory to the field of
intergroup relationships and entertained the possibility that trust in out-groups (i.e., groups who
differ from one's own social or racial group) can be enhanced by comforting interactions with
outgroup members. Specifically, Tropp (2021) suggested that if an outgroup member with whom
people come into contact is responsive to their needs for safety and security, people may feel
20
more secure regarding the outgroup member and more likely to adopt a trusting, collaborative
stance toward him or her. In other words, outgroup-member responsiveness can contribute to the
formation of trust during intergroup contact and then to the formation of more harmonious
intergroup relationships. In support of this view, Tropp (2021) reviewed evidence that
comforting and friendly interactions with outgroup members tend to heighten trust toward the
outgroup and reduce intergroup hostility (e.g., Hässler et al., 2019).
4.4 Sociopolitical Relationships
Besides promoting trust within dyadic or group relationships, the sense of attachment
security can lead people to adopt a trusting orientation toward the organizations to which they
belong (e.g., workplace, social clubs) and the social institutions with which they interact (e.g.,
government, police). Being protected, appreciated, supported, and empowered by their
organization, people may feel secure with respect to this social entity (i.e., more confident in the
availability of organizational support when needed) and therefore might be able to trust in its
goodwill and be willing to be vulnerable to the actions of their organization without being driven
by worries about social exclusion, institutional betrayal, or organizational abuse or maltreatment.
Moreover, people who feel secure with respect to their organization can appreciate its value and
importance in sustaining their own and other members' welfare, enjoy being an integral part of
this benevolent social entity, and feel grateful for its kindness and support. As in dyadic and
group contexts, this heightened relational trust may lead people to reciprocate the support and
attention they receive from an organization and effortfully engage in prosocial activities that
increase the organization's effectiveness and sustainability, and, indirectly, benefit themselves as
members of the organization.
21
Organizations, like relationship partners and groups, can be more or less responsive to
organization members' needs. This kind of responsiveness is a core component of Eisenberger et
al.'s (1986) definition of perceived organizational support, the extent to which people believe
that their organization meets their needs, supports their aspirations, values their contributions,
and cares about their well-being. Resembling our attachment perspective, Eisenberger et al.
(1986) claimed that people's positive beliefs about self and others are strengthened when their
organization is responsive to their needs and its gestures reflect a genuine supportive orientation.
As a result, members of a responsive and supportive organization are likely to develop greater
feelings of trust that future organizational decisions, goals, and plans for change will continue to
take their personal needs into account, that their performance will be continuously appreciated
and rewarded by the organization, and that the organization will not abuse its power.
In support of this view, several studies have found that people who feel more valued,
supported, and empowered by their organization tend to report more trust in the organization and
that this heightened trust explains the positive implications of organizational support for
members' organizational commitment, in-role performance, and pro-organizational behavior
(e.g., Chen et al., 2005). In addition, perceived organizational support has been found to be
associated with lower levels of organizational cynicism -- negative beliefs about the motives and
intentions of an organization (see Chiaburu et al., 2013, for a meta-analysis). According to
Eisenberg et al. (2020), lack of organizational support fosters cynicism “because it lessens the
trust in the organization required to build a solid social exchange relationship” (p. 113).
Another construct related to organizational support is the perception of procedural
justice in an organization, the extent to which people feel they are treated fairly by the
organization (e.g., Greenberg, 1990). According to Tyler and Blader (2003), these perceptions
22
depend on the extent to which (1) the organization treats members with dignity and respect; (2) it
sensitively attends to their needs (i.e., whether they are given voice) within decision-making
procedures; (3) its procedures and decisions are neutral and transparent; and (4) its gestures and
actions convey benevolent and trustworthy motives. It's obvious that these organizational
features can increase perceptions of organizational support and thereby heighten trust in the
organization. Indeed, several studies that have assessed employees' perceptions of procedural
justice in the workplace have yielded moderate-to-strong correlations between these perceptions
and trust in managers and the organization (e.g., Biswas & Kapil, 2017).
According to our attachment perspective, perceptions of organizational support and
procedural justice might result from responsive and supportive organizational actions, but they
can be biased by a person's dominant working models of self and others and his or her
dispositional attachment style. This means that a person's trust in an organization is likely to be a
joint product of organizational actions and the attachment orientations the person brings to
interactions with the organization and its representatives. In their early study of attachment and
work, Hazan and Shaver (1990) found that attachment-insecure employees were more likely than
their secure counterparts to report being misunderstood and underappreciated in their workplace.
Three much more recent studies also found that more attachment-avoidant employees report
lower appraisals of organizational support, fairness, and psychological safety in the workplace
(Byrne et al., 2017; Chopik, 2015; Ronen & Mikulincer, 2009). In addition, more attachment-
anxious employees tend to perceive less procedural justice in their workplace and to hold a more
distrusting stance regarding the extent to which the employing organization will fulfill
contractual obligations (Desivilya et al., 2006; Schmidt, 2016).
23
There is also evidence that attachment security is associated with a behavioral correlate
of trust in an organization: Compliance with its expectations and demands. In two studies
assessing compliance with governmental guidelines for stopping the spread of COVID-19 in
Sweden and Israel, lower attachment anxiety or avoidance in close relationships (i.e., higher
security) predicted greater adherence to these guidelines (Gruneau Brulin et al., 2022; Segal et
al., 2021). Gruneau Brulin et al. (2022) also found that this association was mediated by trust in
governmental institutions. Specifically, more secure participants reported more trust in
government, which in turn contributed to adherence to governmental guidelines.
4.5 Religious/Spiritual Relationships
In extending attachment theory to religious/spiritual relationships, Granqvist (2020)
conceptualized believers' relationship with God and other supernatural figures as an attachment
bond and claimed that believers may perceive God as an especially powerful source of protection
and support (i.e., a safe haven and a secure base). Moreover, believers can feel more or less
secure with regard to the availability of God's support in times of need depending on the sense of
security they generally hold in interpersonal relationships (i.e., generalization of dominant
working models of self and others) and the extent to which interactions with God's earthly
representatives (e.g., clergy, religious communities and institutions, spiritual counselors) result in
feelings of protection, comfort, and empowerment (Granqvist, 2020). It is therefore reasonable to
expect that believers who feel more attachment-secure in close relationships or with respect to
God are more likely to perceive God as a kind and loving figure and to form a trusting
relationship with God.
In one of the earliest studies of attachment and religion, Kirkpatrick and Shaver (1992)
found that people who have a stronger sense of attachment security in human relationships
24
reported more positive perceptions of God as a loving and trustworthy figure. Since then,
numerous studies have replicated this finding in other countries, using different measures of God
images, and across different faith traditions (see Granqvist, 2020, for a review). This association
was also observed in a study using a less explicit measure of God images (Granqvist et al.,
2012). More attachment-secure participants reacted to implicit (preconscious) exposure to the
word “God” (as compared to a neutral word) with faster reactions to positive traits (e.g., loving,
caring) in a lexical decision task and slower reactions to negative traits (e.g., rejecting, distant).
This suggests that attachment security developed in human relationships is indeed associated
with positive mental representations of God. Studies that have assessed patterns of attachment to
God also indicate that greater attachment security with respect to God is associated with stronger
perceptions of God as a loving and trustworthy figure (e.g., Tung et al., 2018).
There is initial evidence that some insecure believers can “earn” a certain degree of trust
in God by reparative experiences within the context of psycho-spiritual interventions aimed at
strengthening beliefs in God's benevolence and responsiveness (see Davis et al., 2021, for a
review). For example, Thomas et al. (2011) reported that an 8-week, spiritually oriented, group-
psychotherapy intervention increased positive images of God and secure attachment to God
among Christian believers who experienced difficulties in trusting God. In another intervention
study involving Iranian adolescents with conduct disorders, 14 sessions of spiritual
psychotherapy (vs. a wait-list condition) reduced negative images of God immediately after the
intervention and generated an increase in attachment security with respect to God that lasted at
least a month (Salmanian et al., 2020). These findings imply that strengthening a secure
attachment to God through religious practices or comforting interactions with God's earthly
25
representatives can lead believers to adopt a more trusting orientation toward God and benefit
from the safety and security that faith and religious doctrines can provide.
Attachment Security and Epistemic Trust
Comforting interactions with responsive attachment figures who reliably provide a safe
haven and secure base might not only increase a person's trust in others' benevolence and
availability in times of need. It might also increase their trust in others' statements and
communicated knowledge (Fonagy & Allison, 2014). In other words, attachment security
contributes to what McCraw (2015) called epistemic trust, the tendency to consider knowledge
that is conveyed by others as significant, relevant to oneself, and generalizable to other contexts.
According to Fonagy and Allison (2014), security-enhancing interactions with responsive
caregivers can reduce children's natural epistemic vigilance, “the self-protective suspicion
towards information coming from others that may be potentially damaging, deceptive, or
inaccurate” (p. 373). Moreover, this kind of interaction creates an opening to an “epistemic
superhighway” (p. 374) by which secure children regard their parents as reliable sources of
knowledge, believing that their statements are provided in a context of authentic care and love.
According to Granqvist (2021), “secure children naturally come to trust the goodwill and
competence of their caregivers, and they can, therefore, use ostensive parental cues as reliable
short-cuts to navigate the environment. … For these reasons, the default position may also
become one of cooperation” (p. 13) (see also Chapter xx).
This conclusion was already evident in Ainsworth et al.'s (1974) analysis of the
socialization process in security-enhancing interactions with loving and caring parents. In their
view, a secure child complies with parents' demands and cooperates with them not because of
fear of punishment or in order to receive a tangible reward but because of the care and attention
26
the child receives from parents and the love the child feels for them. Moreover, by being
understood, validated, and cared for by parents, a secure child learns that attentiveness and
responsiveness to the needs of a relationship partner are the norm. This learning encourages the
child to be attentive and responsive to his or her parents' feelings and needs, to trust in their
communicated knowledge, and to comply with their instructions.
These theoretical ideas have received extensive empirical support. For example, infants
classified as secure at 12 months tend to be more obedient than infants classified as insecure to
their mothers' instructions and to cooperate more with another adult at 21 months (Londerville &
Main, 1981). Kochanska et al. (2010) reported that attachment security at 14-15 months
contributed to greater compliance with parents' instructions at 14 and 22 months; greater
responsiveness to parents' and teachers' demands at 25 and 67 months; and children's more
complete internalization of parental prohibitions at 33, 45, and 56 months. This doesn't mean,
however, that secure children exhibit blind trust or absolute obedience. Corriveau et al. (2009)
found that although secure children were more receptive to their parents' claims than avoidant
children, they still disagreed with parents if the claims the parents made were incorrect (e.g.,
insisting, while following a researcher's instructions, that a somewhat horse-resembling cow was
in fact a horse).
Recently, Campbell et al. (2021) developed a self-report scale to measure adolescents'
and adults' levels of epistemic trust (see al so Chapter xx). The scale comprises three subscales.
The first subscale taps epistemic trust – the extent to which a person relies on others for social
learning (e.g., “I find it very useful to learn from what people tell me about their experiences.”)
The second subscale taps epistemic mistrust, a tendency to treat any source of information as
unreliable or ill-intentioned and to avoid being influenced by others' communications (e.g., “If
27
you put too much faith in what people tell you, you are likely to get hurt”). The third subscale
taps what Campbell et al. (2021) defined as epistemic credulity – “a pronounced lack of
vigilance and discrimination, signaling a general lack of clarity about one's own position and
resulting in vulnerability to misinformation and potential risk of exploitation” (p. 3; e.g., “I have
too often taken advice from the wrong people.”). Findings indicated that more attachment-secure
participants scored higher on epistemic trust and lower on epistemic mistrust and credulity.
Concluding Remarks
In line with Bowlby and Ainsworth's theorizing, the studies we have reviewed here
indicate that attachment security and two major forms of insecurity (attachment anxiety and
avoidance) are closely associated with relational trust. The connections between attachment and
trust have been demonstrated in dyadic, group, sociopolitical, and religious/spiritual
relationships, using both correlational and experimental research designs. It is now important to
branch out in new directions. First, studies should examine times and situations in which
dispositional attachment security in close relationships fails to promote a trusting attitude in
group, sociopolitical, or religious/spiritual relationships. Second, researchers should determine
conditions that may favor establishing relational trust on the part of insecure people. Third,
research should examine how cultural settings and values moderate the link between attachment
security and trust toward social or religious groups, organizations, and institutions. Fourth,
because of the growing emphasis on physiological and neurological underpinnings of
attachment, it will be important to explore how the brain and hormones mediate links between
attachment orientations and the sense of trust. Finally, future studies should test the effects of
clinical and educational interventions aimed at enhancing attachment security in dyadic, group,
28
sociopolitical, and religious/spiritual relationships on the extent to which a person is willing to
extend trust to others even if they are from outside his or her own social, cultural, or racial group.

Attachment, Hope, and Post-traumatic Growth in the Face of Ongoing War
Article
Full-text available
Jul 2026
Dan Confino Dan Confino
Michal Einav Michal Einav
Eyal Rosenstreich Eyal Rosenstreich
Malka Margalit Malka Margalit
Attachment security, reflected in lower levels of attachment anxiety and avoidance, is widely recognized as a key facilitator of post-traumatic growth (PTG) following individual adversity. However, its ability to promote such growth in the context of collective trauma, where both the individual and their significant others are simultaneously affected, remains insufficiently understood. We explore this question by examining the role of key personal and interpersonal resources such as identity fusion, hope, and social acknowledgment as potential buffers against the harmful effects of a collective trauma and as determinants of post-traumatic growth. We surveyed 227 Jewish Israelis at two points in time during their ongoing exposure to the war with Hamas. We administered the initial survey six months after the outbreak of the October 7th war and a second wave, three months afterwards. Results did not reveal an association between changes in attachment anxiety and changes in post-traumatic growth. Of the three potential mediators examined, only hope emerged as a significant mediator and was therefore retained in the final model. Changes in attachment anxiety were significantly associated with changes in hope (a = -0.195, 95% CI [-0.313, -0.077]). In turn, changes in hope were significantly associated with changes in PTG (b = 0.200, 95% CI [0.055, 0.344]). Beyond their theoretical contribution to the post-traumatic growth literature, these findings may help practitioners working with individuals coping with collective trauma design trauma-related interventions, such as those focusing on hope and attachment behaviors.

BUILDING POSITIVE RELATIONSHIPS: THE ROLE OF EMPATHY AND COMPASSION IN PERSONAL GROWTH
Article
Full-text available
Apr 2026
Liu Yang
Chen Mei
Ethan Tan
In today's increasingly interconnected and diverse world, the ability to build positive relationships is essential for both personal and professional success. Empathy and compassion are two core interpersonal skills that contribute to stronger connections and greater well-being. These qualities not only enhance relationships but also promote personal growth by fostering understanding, emotional resilience, and a sense of shared humanity. However, the specific role of empathy and compassion in personal development remains underexplored. This study aims to examine the role of empathy and compassion in building positive relationships and promoting personal growth. The research investigates how these two traits influence emotional intelligence, self-awareness, and interpersonal communication in diverse contexts. A mixed-methods approach was employed, combining quantitative surveys and qualitative interviews. Data were collected from 250 participants across various age groups and professions. The findings revealed that higher levels of empathy and compassion were associated with improved interpersonal relationships and greater personal growth. Participants who reported stronger empathy and compassion exhibited better emotional regulation, higher self-awareness, and more positive social interactions. This study concludes that empathy and compassion are integral to building positive relationships and fostering personal growth.

Dika Sahputra Dika Sahputra
Andika Fawri

Background. The quality of parental closeness, characterized by trust, effective communication, and low levels of alienation, is considered a protective factor in fostering academic resilience Purpose. This study aims to analyze the determination of the quality of parental closeness on students' academic resilience in an era of high academic pressure. Increasing academic demands, competition, and performance expectations require students to possess strong adaptive abilities in order to survive and achieve academic success. Method. This study employed a quantitative approach with a sample of 140 university students. Data were collected using a parental closeness scale and an academic resilience scale, and were analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistical techniques. Results. The results indicated that the quality of parental closeness was generally in the moderate to high category, with trust emerging as the most dominant dimension. Meanwhile, the level of students' academic resilience was predominantly in the moderate category (56.429%), followed by the high category (37.143%), suggesting that most students have a fairly good capacity to cope with academic pressure. Conclusion. These findings indicate that the higher the quality of parental closeness, the stronger the students' academic resilience. Supportive relationships provide a sense of security, emotional support, and psychological resources that help students manage stress and academic challenges in an adaptive manner.

The present study attempted to find empirical connections between the attachment, object-relations, and triangular love perspectives as they apply to relationship with God. Attachment to God and object-relations perspectives on God have already been extensively investigated in the literature. In this study, it was observed that the triangular love model (Sternberg, 1986) could also be applied to ... [Show full abstract] relationship with God. Using established instruments from each literature—attachment, object-relations, triangular love—it was observed that two factors best explained the correlations among these instruments. The first factor, “Communion,” describes the degree of intimacy, closeness, dependency, and trust in the God-relationship. The second factor, “Complaint,” describes the degree of disappointment and/or frustration involved in the God-relationship. Because these two factors—Communion and Complaint—are orthogonal, it is argued that the commingling of Communion and Complaint in the God-relationship is one feature that can imbue this relationship with an emotional dynamic similar to that observed in human love relationships.

An Overview of Adult Attachment Theory 
Phillip R. Shaver Mario Mikulincer 
Bowlby and Ainsworth’s attachment theory (Ainsworth, Blehar, Waters, & Wall, 1978; Bowlby, 1969/1982) is one of the most successful psychological theories of the past half century. It has generated thousands of published studies and scores of books. It has appealed to all kinds of psychologists, including developmentalists, clinicians, personality and social psychologists, and even psychologists who study groups and organizations (see Mikulincer & Shaver, 2007, for a broad overview). There are several reasons for the theory’s success. 
First, attachment theory has roots in psychoanalysis, cognitive-develop-mental psychology, control systems theory, and primate ethology. No other theory is so deeply and broadly grounded in earlier conceptualizations of the social aspects of the human and nonhuman primate mind. 
Second, the theory was expounded unusually clearly and systematically by Bowlby in his Attachment and Loss trilogy (Bowlby, 1969/1982, 1973, 1980). Most other psychoanalytic theorists had written (perhaps deliberately) in a convoluted and opaque manner, and their concepts (e.g., the id, cathexes, the death instinct) were difficult for researchers to operationalize. Bowlby reviewed diverse bodies of research and theory, somehow integrating them seamlessly and retaining both the depth and complexity of psychoanalytic ideas without losing track of the need for empirical grounding. Even Bowlby’s boldest speculations were solidly rooted in established science. 
Third, although Bowlby was primarily a clinician and a clinical theorist rather than a researcher, his close collaboration with Ainsworth resulted in measures and research paradigms that appealed to less clinical but empiri-

18 THEORETICAL FOUNDATIONS 
cally oriented researchers. No other object relations clinical theorist established a partnership with an astute observer and laboratory researcher like Ainsworth. Hence most of the other object relations theorists’ ideas (whether good or bad—a distinction that is impossible to draw without evidence) have fallen by the wayside as empirical psychology has advanced. In contrast, attachment theory has continued to guide creative research—and, with Bowlby’s blessings (see, e.g., Bowlby, 1988), the theory has continued to evolve in response to new research paradigms and findings. 
The present chapter is an attempt to boil down the current version of the theory, especially as it applies to adults, to a workable set of ideas and constructs that will recur throughout the remaining chapters. A much more detailed examination of the same large territory, including a nearly exhaustive literature review, can be found in our recent book (Mikulincer & Shaver, 2007). At the end of the present chapter, we briefly consider the ways in which Bowlby and Ainsworth’s theory is compatible with but different from other psychological frameworks that have guided clinical practice, including Freudian psychoanalysis, behaviorism, cognitivism, and structural approaches to the analysis of social relationships. 
THE ATTACHMENT BEHAVIORAL SYSTEM 
We begin by covering the normative (species-universal) aspects of what Bowlby (1969/1982, 1973, 1980) called the attachment behavioral system. Attachment theorists and researchers are all familiar with a set of standard names for the theory’s basic constructs, and we define and discuss these constructs in this section. 
According to Bowlby (1969/1982), human infants are born with a repertoire of behaviors (attachment behaviors) “designed” by evolution to assure proximity to supportive others (attachment figures), who are likely to provide protection from physical and psychological threats, promote safe and healthy exploration of the environment, and help the infant learn to regulate emotions effectively. The child’s proximity-seeking behaviors are organized by an adaptive behavioral system (the attachment behavioral system), which emerged over the course of evolution because it increased the likelihood of survival and reproduction in a species whose offspring are born with very immature abilities to acquire food, move about their environment, or defend themselves (from predators, stressors, and other dangers). This system is assumed to govern the choice, activation, and termination of proximity-seeking behaviors aimed at attaining protection and support from significant others in times of need. Although the attachment system is most important early in life, Bowlby (1988) claimed that it is active across the lifespan and is manifest in thoughts and behaviors related to proximity seeking in times of need. This claim provided the impetus for subsequent theorists and researchers to conceptualize and study adult attachment.

 An Overview of Adult Attachment Theory 19 
During infancy, primary caregivers (usually one or both parents, but also grandparents, neighbors, older siblings, day care workers, etc.) are likely to occupy the role of attachment figure. Ainsworth (1973) reported that infants tend to seek proximity to their primary caregiver when tired or ill, and Heinicke and Westheimer (1966) found that infants tend to be soothed in the presence of their primary caregivers. During adolescence and adulthood, other relationship partners often become targets of proximity seeking and emotional support, including close friends and romantic partners. Teachers and supervisors in academic settings or therapists in clinical settings can also serve as real or potential sources of comfort and support. Moreover, groups, institutions, and symbolic personages (e.g., God, the Bud-dha, the Virgin Mary) can be recruited as attachment figures. As a group, these real people and symbolic personages form what Bowlby (1969/1982) called a person’s hierarchy of attachment figures. 
In addition, mental representations of attachment figures and subroutines of the self that develop through the internalization of caring and soothing qualities of attachment figures can successfully provide a symbolic sense of comfort, support, and protection (Mikulincer & Shaver, 2004). They can also serve as internalized models of effective, loving behavior that guide a person in helping him- or herself in the absence of physically present attachment figures. 
From an attachment perspective, a specific relationship partner is an attachment figure and a specific relationship is an attachment relationship only to the extent that a relationship partner accomplishes three important functions (e.g., Ainsworth, 1991; Hazan & Shaver, 1994; Hazan & Zeif-man, 1994). First, the attachment figure should be viewed as a target for proximity seeking in times of stress or need, and unwanted separation from this person should elicit distress, protest, and efforts to achieve reunion. Second, the person should be viewed as a real or potential safe haven, because he or she provides comfort, support, protection, and security in times of need. Third, the person should be viewed as a secure base, allowing a child or adult to pursue non-attachment-related goals in a safe environment and to sustain exploration, risk taking, and self-expansion. In other words, interactions with attachment figures are not the same as other forms of social interaction. Attachment-related interactions are organized around the expectation of receiving protection, comfort, encouragement, or support from an attachment figure in times of need, and this protection or support is valued because it allows a person to restore emotional balance and return to effective behavior in the wider social and physical environment. 
What attachment theory calls activation of the attachment system can be seen in the behavior of human infants, who tend to drop whatever they are doing (e.g., playing with interesting toys in a laboratory situation) and seek comfort and support from an attachment figure if an odd noise is heard or a stranger enters the room (Ainsworth et al., 1978). The same kind of activation is notable in the minds of adults who are subjected to conscious

20 THEORETICAL FOUNDATIONS 
or unconscious threats. For example, we (Mikulincer, Gillath, & Shaver, 2002) conducted several experiments in which we subliminally presented threatening words (e.g., failure, separation) to adults and then assessed indi-rectly (using reaction times in a word identification task or word-color-nam-ing task) which names of relationship partners became more available for mental processing following the unconscious threat. It turned out that the names of attachment figures (identified with the WHOTO questionnaire, developed by Hazan & Zeifman, 1994, and adapted by Fraley & Davis, 1997, and Trinke & Bartholomew, 1997) became more available following unconscious exposure to a threatening word. The threatening words had no effect on the mental availability or accessibility of names of other people who were not viewed as attachment figures. That is, attachment figures are not just any relationship partners; they are special people to whom one turns, even unconsciously, when comfort or support is needed. 
According to Bowlby (1969/1982), the natural goal of the attachment system is to increase a person’s sense of security (which Sroufe & Waters, 1977, labeled felt security)—a sense that the world is a safe place, that one can rely on others for protection and support, and that one can confidently explore the environment and engage in social and nonsocial tasks and activities without fear of damage. This goal is made particularly salient by encountering actual or symbolic threats, or by appraising an attachment figure as not sufficiently available or responsive. In such cases, the attachment system is activated and the individual is driven to reestablish actual or symbolic proximity to an attachment figure (which attachment researchers call the primary strategy of the attachment system; Main, 1990). These bids for proximity persist until the sense of security is restored, at which time the attachment system is deactivated or turned down in “volume,” and the individual calmly and skillfully returns to other activities. That is, the search for support, protection, and security is not only a goal in itself, but also an important foundation for attaining many non-attachment-related goals. 
During infancy, the primary attachment strategy includes nonverbal expressions of neediness, such as crying and pleading, and movements (crawling, walking, extending arms) aimed at reestablishing and maintaining proximity to the caregiver (Ainsworth et al., 1978). In adulthood, this attachment strategy includes many other methods of establishing contact (e.g., talking, calling someone on the telephone, sending an e-mail or text message), as well as mentally activating soothing, comforting representations of attachment figures or even self-representations associated with these figures (Mikulincer & Shaver, 2004). Such cognitive–affective representations can infuse a person with a heightened sense of security and allow him or her to continue pursuing other goals without having to interrupt them to engage in actual bids for proximity and protection. 
Indeed, several studies (e.g., Green & Campbell, 2000; Mikulincer, Hirschberger, Nachmias, & Gillath, 2001; Mikulincer & Shaver, 2001; Miku-lincer, Shaver, Gillath, & Nitzberg, 2005) have shown that a variety of experi-

mental techniques designed to activate mental representations of attachment figures (e.g., subliminal presentation of the names of people nominated as attachment figures in the WHOTO questionnaire; visualization of the faces of these figures) infuse a person with positive affect; reduce hostility to outgroup members; facilitate empathy, compassion, and altruistic helping; and sustain relaxed and creative forms of exploration. They also reduce the stridency of hurt feelings among anxious individuals and open more avoidant individuals to such feelings that have been suppressed (Shaver, Mikulincer, Lavy, & Cassidy, in press), both of which are likely to be very useful clinically. 
Bowlby (1988) summarized many of the adaptive benefits of proximity seeking. First, he viewed successful bids for proximity and the attainment of felt security as necessary for forming and maintaining successful relationships. Every attachment-related interaction that restores a person’s sense of security reaffirms the value of closeness and strengthens affectional bonds with the relationship partner responsible for augmenting the sense of security. Moreover, successful bids for proximity and support play an important part in teaching a person how to regulate and deescalate negative emotions, such as anger, anxiety, and sadness (Bowlby, 1973, 1980). They therefore help a person maintain emotional balance and resilience in the face of stress. Bowlby (1973) also viewed attachment security as an important foundation for developing skills and competence of all kinds. A child or adult who feels threatened and inadequately protected or supported has a difficult time directing attention to free play, curious investigation of objects and environments, and affiliative relationships with peers. Extended over long periods of time, this kind of interference disrupts the development of self-efficacy, self-esteem, and positive, trusting social attitudes. Because of Bowl-by’s (1969/1982) emphasis on the value of felt security, he strongly rejected any theoretical formulation that equated attachment per se with excessive dependence or childishness. In his view, secure attachment provides a foundation for personal growth and mature autonomy, which should never be equated with a reduction in the importance of close relationships. In his estimation, claims that well-treated children are likely to be “spoiled” or overly dependent confuse anxious attachment with attachment per se. 
INDIVIDUAL DIFFERENCES IN ATTACHMENT SYSTEM FUNCTIONING 
Attachment theory is a general theory of social and emotional development, but it would probably not have captured the attention of developmental, personality, social, and clinical researchers if it had been only that. What captured research psychologists’ attention were the patterns or styles of attachment emphasized in Bowlby’s theory and operationalized in Ains-worth’s research on mother–infant dyads. Most of the research and clinical applications inspired by the theory deal with these individual differences.

22 THEORETICAL FOUNDATIONS 
Attachment Figure Availability and Secondary  Attachment Strategies 
Besides possessing a species-universal set of operating characteristics, the attachment behavioral system includes various regulatory parameters that can be influenced by a person’s history of interactions with key attachment figures. In early infancy, the effects of experience can be conceptualized in terms of simple learning principles. If a particular behavioral strategy (e.g., crying for help, protesting angrily, down-regulating distress signals) works with a particular caregiver, it will be reinforced. If a particular strategy results in punishment or caregiver withdrawal, it will become weaker and less visible (perhaps by being actively suppressed) in the infant’s behavioral repertoire. The same is true for young mammals from many other species. 
In the case of developing human children, however, what is learned includes not only automatic behavior patterns, but also a set of vivid memories, abstracted beliefs, and expectations about caregivers’ reactions and the effectiveness or ineffectiveness of one’s own possible behaviors. Because Bowlby and Ainsworth were writing at about the time of what has been called, in retrospect, the “cognitive revolution” in psychology, they were sensitive to the role played by memories, cognitive schemas, and other mental representations in regulating the attachment system. In attachment the-ory, these mental structures and processes are called internal working models of self and others (Bartholomew, 1990; Bowlby, 1969/1982). Over time, a person’s working models, which contain both conscious and unconscious elements, become molded by the quality of interactions with attachment figures; that is, the system is “programmed” to fit these figures’ characteristic behaviors, thereby increasing the likelihood of reliable expectations and effective reactions in those particular relational environments. Through this process, a person learns to adjust his or her attachment system to fit contextual demands and rely on expectations about possible access routes to protection and security. These working models are thought to be the basis of both current individual differences in attachment strategies, or styles, and within-person continuity in the operation of the attachment system over time. 
According to Bowlby (1973, 1988), variations in working models, and hence in attachment system functioning, depend on the availability, sensitivity, and responsiveness of attachment figures in times of need. When one’s key relationship partner is available, sensitive, and responsive to one’s prox-imity- and support-seeking efforts, one is likely to experience felt security and to have greater confidence in proximity seeking as an effective distress regulation strategy. During such interactions one also acquires procedural knowledge about distress management, which we can imagine being organized around a relational script (Waters, Rodrigues, & Ridgeway, 1998). This secure-base script includes something like the following “if–then” propositions: “If I encounter an obstacle and/or become distressed, I can

 An Overview of Adult Attachment Theory 23 
approach a significant other for help; he or she is likely to be available and supportive; I will experience relief and comfort as a result of proximity to this person; I can then return to other activities.” 
However, when a primary attachment figure proves not to be available, sensitive, or responsive, felt security is not attained, and the distress that initially activated proximity-seeking efforts is compounded by serious attach-ment-related doubts (e.g., “Can I trust others in times of need?”). These frightening, frustrating interactions also signal that the primary attachment strategy is failing to accomplish its goal and that alternative strategies must be adopted to deal with current insecurities and distress. Attachment theorists (e.g., Cassidy & Kobak, 1988; Main, 1990) have called these alterna-tive tactics secondary attachment strategies, which (based on Ainsworth et al.’s [1978] research) are thought to take two major forms: hyperactivation and deactivation. 
Hyperactivated strategies are what Bowlby (1969/1982) called protest reactions to the frustration of attachment needs. Protest often occurs in relationships in which the attachment figure is sometimes responsive but unreliably so, placing the needy individual on a partial reinforcement schedule that seems to reward persistence of energetic, strident, noisy proximity-seeking attempts, because such attempts sometimes seem to succeed. In such cases, the individual does not give up on frustrating proximity-seeking bids, but in fact intensifies them to demand or coerce the attachment figure’s attention, love, and support. The main goal of these strategies is to make an unreliable or insufficiently available and responsive figure provide support and security. The way to pursue this goal seems, to the hyperactivating individual, to be to keep his or her attachment system in a chronically activated state until support and comfort is attained. This involves exaggerating appraisals of danger and signs of the attachment figure’s unavailability, and intensifying one’s demands for attention, care, and love. It can, paradoxically, lead to intensifying one’s needs, and emotional reactions to frustrated needs, as a way of “regulating” them (even though the term emotion regulation in psychological writings usually refers to down-regulation of negative emotions). 
Deactivating strategies, in contrast, are efforts to escape, avoid, or minimize the pain and frustration caused by unavailable, unsympathetic, or unresponsive attachment figures. This kind of response seems to occur in relationships with attachment figures who disapprove of and punish closeness and expressions of need, dependence, and vulnerability. In such relationships, a needy individual learns to expect better outcomes if proximityseeking bids are suppressed, the attachment system is deactivated, and one attempts to deal with threats and dangers alone. Bowlby (1969/1982) called this strategy compulsive self-reliance. The primary goal of deactivating strategies is to keep the attachment system turned off or down-regulated to avoid recurring frustration and distress arising from interactions with cold, neglectful, or punishing attachment figures.
